summary: The note surveys the folklore and history of sea serpents and the Kraken, from Norse sagas and early modern maps and natural histories to 19th-century sightings and scientific explanations such as giant squid. It also covers modern media portrayals, tourism and festivals, and why these maritime myths endure as reflections of human fear and fascination.
one_line: An overview of sea serpent and Kraken legends, tracing their origins in Norse myth, early sightings, scientific explanations, modern media and cultural tourism.
key_facts: Historical accounts as early as 1000 AD describe sailors and fishermen claiming to see elongated sea serpents with scaled bodies and terrifying eyes.
A Norse saga dated November 12, 1021 describes 'Jörmungandr', a serpent so large it encircled the earth, holding its tail in its mouth.
The Midgard Serpent (Jörmungandr) was an offspring of the trickster god Loki.
Olaus Magnus's "Carta Marina", created January 15, 1539, shows a serpent attacking a ship off the coast of Scandinavia.
An old Icelandic saga describes a whale-like beast called 'Hafgufa', an early precursor of the Kraken.
Abbot Pontoppidan, on September 23, 1755, gave the creature the name 'Kraken' and said it was seen off Norway and Greenland.
Alfred Tennyson published the poem "The Kraken" on April 2, 1830, depicting a colossal beast slumbering in the abyss.
Conrad Gesner's "Historiae animalium", published May 21, 1558, is a compendium of marine monsters including sea serpents.
Captain Richard Whitbourne's journal of June 4, 1610 recorded a 'furious and terrible sea dragon' off Newfoundland.
On August 28, 1848, Captain Peter M'Quhae of the HMS Daedalus reported an enormous serpentine creature, reigniting scientific interest.
Misidentified animals such as oarfish or certain sharks are proposed explanations for sea serpent sightings.
A colossal squid find on February 3, 2007 provided a real-world analog to the Kraken myth.
The Kraken's first appearance in the 'Pirates of the Caribbean' franchise is noted as September 7, 2006.
The annual Sea Serpent Festival in Aberdeen, Scotland is scheduled next for October 15, 2024.
